title: Closed and bounded is not enough

prereqs.why: The definition by open covers is what the options are testing.
Three of the options describe sets as closed, and that has to be checked in the right space.
The discrete metric is the counterexample that separates the two conditions.

statement:
A metric space $X$ is **compact** if every open cover of $X$ has a finite subcover.

In $\R^n$, the Heine–Borel theorem says this is equivalent to being closed and bounded. That equivalence is a **theorem about $\R^n$**, not a definition, and it fails elsewhere.

Which of these spaces is **compact**?
hints: Compactness is about covers. For each option, either produce a finite subcover of an arbitrary cover, or find one cover with no finite subcover.
For the infinite discrete space, the single-point balls $B(x,\tfrac12) = \{x\}$ form an open cover. How many of them can you throw away?
Heine–Borel applies to subsets of $\R^n$ with the usual metric — and to nothing else on this list. Check which option is actually of that form.

options: $\R$ with the metric $\rho(x,y) = \min(|x-y|, 1)$, which is bounded by $1$ and in which $\R$ is closed.
